q: Name the pinned nerve, which keeps the external urethral sphincter contracted.

fig.alt: A side view of the female pelvis cut down the midline, with the sacrum at the back and the pubic bone at the front. The bladder sits behind the pubic bone. Nerves leave the sacral part of the spinal cord through the sacrum and run forward and down; they join to form the pudendal nerve, which reaches the ring of muscle around the urethra, labeled sphincter, and the skin and muscle of the genital region. q: Order the arteries that carry blood into the kidney, starting at the aorta.
Order the structures a drop of urine passes through after it drips from a renal papilla, until it leaves the body.
Order the steps of the micturition reflex, from a filling bladder to urine flowing.
options: The bladder wall stretches as urine collects
Stretch-sensitive sensory endings send signals to the sacral cord and the pons
The cortex releases the pontine micturition center
Pudendal firing falls and the external urethral sphincter relaxes
Parasympathetic fibers from the sacral micturition center fire
The detrusor contracts and the internal urethral sphincter opens

q: Fill the gap in the arterial path: renal artery → segmental artery → ____ → arcuate artery → cortical radiate artery.
List the three coverings of the kidney in order, from the outside in.
options: Renal capsule, adipose capsule, renal fascia
Adipose capsule, renal fascia, renal capsule
Renal fascia, renal capsule, adipose capsule
Renal fascia, adipose capsule, renal capsule

q: A clot blocks one segmental artery in a patient's right kidney. A scan a week later shows a wedge-shaped area of dead tissue with its broad side at the kidney's surface. Why did no other artery keep that area alive?
options: The renal vein carried the clot back into that segment
Segmental arteries are end arteries that do not connect with one another
The cortex has no capillaries of its own
The adipose capsule compresses the arteries around the segment

q: A surgeon removes a patient's kidney through a cut in the flank and back, without ever opening the peritoneal cavity. Which fact about the kidney makes this possible?
options: It is suspended in the peritoneal cavity by a mesentery
It sits below the level of the iliac crest
It lies behind the peritoneum, against the muscles of the back wall
It is enclosed by the ribs on all sides

q: When the bladder contracts, why is urine not pushed back up the ureters toward the kidneys?
options: Each ureter has a ring of skeletal muscle that closes it
The ureters pass through the bladder wall at a slant, and bladder pressure squeezes them shut
The trigone contracts first and seals the bladder floor, including both ureter openings
Peristalsis stops in the ureters whenever you are lying down

q: Bacteria from the skin reach the bladder much more often in women than in men. Which anatomical difference best explains this?
options: The female bladder has no trigone
The female urethra has no external sphincter
The female urethra is about 3 to 4 cm long, the male about 20 cm
The female ureters enter the front of the bladder instead of the back

q: A patient with an overactive bladder takes a drug that blocks muscarinic receptor proteins. Predict how each variable changes compared with before the drug.

variables.name: Volume the bladder holds before an urgent need to empty
Strength of the external urethral sphincter
Volume left in the bladder after emptying

q: Why does the right kidney usually sit a little lower than the left?
options: The liver occupies the space above it
The aorta lies on the right side of the spine
It is larger and heavier than the left

q: A student wrote the path of urine from a pyramid to the bladder. One step is wrong. Which one?
Which statements about the urinary bladder are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Its smooth muscle is called the detrusor
It is lined by transitional epithelium that folds into rugae when empty
The trigone lies between the two ureter openings and the urethral opening
It lies in the pelvic cavity, behind the pubic bone
The trigone is where the lining folds most as the bladder empties

q: After an injury to the nerves of the pelvic floor, a patient can no longer tighten the muscle she used to squeeze to hold in urine, although her bladder still contracts normally when she empties it. Which structure has lost its nerve supply?
options: The detrusor muscle, supplied by parasympathetic fibers
The internal urethral sphincter, supplied by sympathetic fibers
The trigone, supplied by sensory fibers
The external urethral sphincter, via the pudendal nerve

q: At rest, the kidneys receive about 20 to 25 percent of cardiac output, although they weigh less than half a percent of the body. What is that flow mainly for?
options: Supplying the kidney cells with oxygen for their own work
Warming the blood before it returns to the heart
Storing a reserve of blood for use during bleeding
Providing the plasma from which urine is made

q: Order the parts of the nephron that filtered fluid flows through, starting where it is first collected.
options: Descending limb of the nephron loop
Ascending limb of the nephron loop

q: Order the vessels blood passes through, from a cortical radiate artery to a cortical radiate vein, in a cortical nephron.
Fill the gap: afferent arteriole → glomerulus → ____ → peritubular capillaries.
misconception: blood leaving the glomerulus enters a venule

q: A student listed the path of filtered fluid through a nephron. One step is wrong. Which one?
options: Ascending limb of the nephron loop

q: Under the microscope, one part of the tubule has cuboidal cells with a dense brush border of microvilli and very many mitochondria. What does this structure suggest about its job?
options: It lets water through passively, without spending any ATP at all
It releases renin into the blood
It moves large amounts of material back into the blood

q: Which are parts of the renal corpuscle? Select all that apply.
options: Parietal layer of the glomerular capsule

q: Which feature sets a juxtamedullary nephron apart from a cortical nephron?
options: It has no proximal convoluted tubule at all, only a loop
Its renal corpuscle lies in the medulla
It drains straight into the renal pelvis
A long loop that reaches deep into the medulla, with vasa recta beside it

q: The kangaroo rat lives in the desert without drinking water and makes urine several times more concentrated than human urine. Which feature would you expect its kidneys to have?
options: Mostly cortical nephrons with short loops and a thin medulla
Very long nephron loops reaching deep into the medulla

q: Why is blood pressure in the glomerular capillaries much higher than in capillaries elsewhere, such as in your skin?
options: The glomerulus is close to the heart
The glomerular capillaries have thicker walls than other capillaries
An arteriole on the way out holds pressure back in the glomerulus
The podocytes pump blood through the capillaries

q: A patient bleeds heavily, and pressure in her afferent arterioles falls. Which cells respond directly to this fall by releasing renin?
options: Macula densa cells in the tubule wall
Cells of the proximal convoluted tubule next to the capsule
Juxtaglomerular cells in the wall of the afferent arteriole

q: Which structure receives fluid from many nephrons?
What is a podocyte?
options: A cell of the capsule's visceral layer that wraps the glomerular capillaries
A smooth muscle cell in the afferent arteriole wall that stores and releases renin
A cell of the macula densa that senses sodium chloride
A flat cell of the capsule's outer wall

q: A tiny clot completely blocks the afferent arteriole of one nephron. Predict the change in each variable for that nephron, compared with before the clot.

variables.name: Blood flow in the peritubular capillaries fed by its efferent arteriole
Blood flow into the glomerulus of a neighboring nephron

q: What do mesangial cells inside the glomerulus do?
options: They support the capillary loops, can contract, and engulf trapped debris
They release renin into the blood
They sense sodium chloride in the tubule fluid

q: A person loses half of their nephrons over several years. Blood tests stay nearly normal for a long time. Which explanation fits what you know about nephrons?
options: New nephrons grow to replace the lost ones
The surviving nephrons each filter and process more fluid
The collecting ducts take over filtering blood
The bladder begins to take back water and salt

options: It doubles, because more pressure is in the system
It stops, because net filtration pressure falls to 0
It is unchanged, because only the glomerular pressure matters
It rises, because capsular pressure pushes fluid out

q: A patient's kidneys have a filtration coefficient of 12 mL/min per mm Hg and a net filtration pressure of 8 mm Hg. What is the GFR?

variables.name: Hydrostatic pressure in the peritubular capillaries

variables.name: Colloid osmotic pressure in the peritubular capillaries

q: A person's mean arterial pressure rises from point B (100 mm Hg) to 160 mm Hg during a stressful moment. Read the solid curve. What happens to GFR?

It falls, because the arterioles close completely
It rises past 150 mL/min, as on the dashed line

Point A is on the curve at 60 mm Hg, point B on the plateau at 100 mm Hg, and point C at 190 mm Hg.

q: After a heavy bleed, a patient's mean arterial pressure is at point A (60 mm Hg). Why is GFR there so far below normal, although it is higher than the dashed line?

Autoregulation has switched off completely below 80 mm Hg
The afferent arterioles are already fully widened, and pressure is too low to keep GFR at normal
Capsular hydrostatic pressure has risen above glomerular pressure

q: Name the pinned gaps between the podocytes' interlocking branches.

(b) One capillary with three of these cells wrapped around it; the cell bodies, the capillary and the slits between the interlocking processes are labeled.

q: Name the pinned pores in the capillary wall.

q: A cyclist is hit by a car and loses about 1.5 L of blood. His urine output drops sharply over the next hour. What best explains the fall in GFR?
options: Strong sympathetic activation constricts his afferent arterioles
ANP released by stretched atria dilates his afferent arterioles
His plasma proteins fall, so colloid osmotic pressure pulls fluid in
Tubuloglomerular feedback dilates his afferent arterioles

q: After three days of vomiting, a woman who is low on fluid takes high doses of ibuprofen for a headache. Her GFR falls sharply. Why does the ibuprofen matter more for her than for a healthy person?
options: Ibuprofen damages the podocytes and blocks the filtration slits
Ibuprofen constricts the efferent arterioles directly
Her afferent arterioles depend on prostaglandins to stay open

q: Mr. Osei has narrowed arteries to both kidneys. After he starts an ACE inhibitor, his GFR falls by half. Which change in his glomeruli explains this?
options: Less angiotensin II lets his efferent arterioles relax, so glomerular pressure falls
Less angiotensin II constricts his afferent arterioles
The drug makes his filtration membrane less permeable
More aldosterone makes his tubules keep sodium

q: Which substances pass freely from the blood into the glomerular filtrate? Select all that apply.
Order the steps of tubuloglomerular feedback after a nephron's GFR rises.
options: Filtrate flows faster through the tubule
More sodium chloride reaches the macula densa
The macula densa releases ATP, broken down to adenosine

q: Fill the gap in the layers of the filtration membrane, from the blood side: fenestrated endothelium → ____ → filtration slits between podocyte pedicels.
A student wrote the myogenic mechanism for a rise in blood pressure. One step is wrong. Which one?
options: The wall of the afferent arteriole is stretched
Mechanically gated channels open and calcium enters the smooth muscle
Glomerular hydrostatic pressure stays near normal

q: A man with long-standing diabetes mellitus has foamy urine that tests strongly positive for protein, and his ankles and eyelids have become puffy. What links his urine to his swelling?
options: Protein in the urine irritates the bladder and triggers fluid retention
His glomeruli filter less fluid, so water that should leave in the urine builds up in his tissues
Lost albumin lowers blood colloid osmotic pressure, so capillaries filter more fluid out
Protein in the filtrate raises capsular pressure and forces fluid into the veins

q: A urine sample contains red blood cells that are misshapen and packed into cylinder-shaped plugs, along with a lot of protein. Where is the bleeding most likely coming from?
A patient's renal plasma flow is 600 mL/min and his GFR is 120 mL/min. What is his filtration fraction?
Blood colloid osmotic pressure is about 25 mm Hg as blood enters a glomerulus but about 35 mm Hg as it leaves. What causes the rise?
options: The liver adds albumin to the blood inside the glomerulus
Protein-free fluid is filtered out, concentrating the proteins left behind
Podocytes secrete protein into the capillaries
Blood cells break down and release their protein as they pass through the capillary loops

q: A fast IV infusion stretches a patient's atria, and they release ANP. What does ANP do to GFR, and how?
options: Lowers it, by constricting the afferent arteriole
Raises it, by widening the afferent arteriole and relaxing mesangial cells
Lowers it, by making mesangial cells contract and shrink the filtering surface
No change, because ANP acts only on the heart

q: A resting person's mean arterial pressure falls suddenly from 100 to 85 mm Hg and stays there. Predict each variable about a minute later, after autoregulation has acted, compared with before the fall.
About how much glomerular filtrate do the two kidneys of a healthy young adult make?
Which layer of the filtration membrane stops blood cells from entering the filtrate?
options: The parietal layer of the capsule

q: A woman's glomeruli filter 170 L a day and she passes 1.7 L of urine. What percentage of the filtered water does her renal tubule reabsorb?
A man's GFR is 180 L/day and his plasma sodium is 140 mmol/L. He excretes 200 mmol of sodium a day. How much sodium does his tubule reabsorb each day?
A toxin blocks the sodium–potassium pumps of proximal tubule cells. None of the apical glucose carriers uses ATP. What happens to glucose reabsorption?
options: It stops, as cell sodium rises and the inward sodium gradient disappears
It continues unchanged, since the glucose carriers need no ATP
It speeds up, as sodium builds up inside the cell and drives the carriers harder
It switches to the paracellular route between the cells

q: Which segment of the renal tubule reabsorbs the largest share of filtered sodium and water?
Use the graph. At a plasma glucose of 600 mg/dL, about how much glucose is excreted in urine each minute?

fig.alt: A graph of glucose handling by both kidneys against plasma glucose concentration from 0 to 800 mg/dL. The filtered load rises in a straight line from 0 to 1,000 mg/min. The reabsorbed amount follows the filtered load exactly up to about 180 mg/dL, then bends over and levels off at the transport maximum of about 375 mg/min from about 350 mg/dL upward. The excreted amount is zero up to about 180 mg/dL, the renal threshold, then rises, running parallel to the filtered load once reabsorption has leveled off. A marker at 90 mg/dL shows a normal fasting glucose, where all filtered glucose is reabsorbed.

q: Mr. Mensah, 52, has undiagnosed diabetes mellitus. His plasma glucose is 280 mg/dL, and his urine dipstick shows glucose. His kidneys are healthy. Why is glucose in his urine?
options: His glomeruli have been damaged by diabetes and now let glucose through
His tubules secrete excess glucose into the urine
Some nephrons get more glucose than their carriers can reabsorb
Insulin is needed for the tubule to reabsorb glucose

q: Glucose's transport maximum is 375 mg/min and GFR is 125 mL/min, so glucose should first appear in urine at 3 mg/mL (300 mg/dL). It actually appears at about 180 mg/dL. What explains the difference?
options: Nephrons differ, and those with fewer carriers saturate first
GFR rises when glucose is high, pushing extra glucose through
Some glucose is secreted into the tubule even at normal levels
The transport maximum falls whenever glucose rises

q: A benign tumor of the zona glomerulosa releases large amounts of aldosterone. Predict the change in each variable, compared with before the tumor.

variables.name: Number of open sodium channels in principal cells
Sodium reabsorbed in the collecting duct
Glucose reabsorbed in the proximal tubule

q: Put the steps in order to show how a glucose molecule in the filtrate returns to the blood.

Sodium flows into the cell down its gradient on a symporter, carrying glucose with it
Glucose builds up inside the cell above its level in the interstitial fluid
Glucose leaves the cell across the basolateral membrane by facilitated diffusion
Glucose moves from the interstitial fluid into a peritubular capillary

q: Select every substance the renal tubule secretes into the tubular fluid.

Most of the potassium leaks back into the lumen through potassium channels
The lumen becomes positively charged, pushing calcium and magnesium out between the cells
Water follows the salt out of the tubule by osmosis
The fluid leaving the segment is more dilute than plasma

q: Complete the kidney's mass balance: amount excreted = amount filtered − amount reabsorbed + amount ____.
A drug blocks the action of aldosterone in the collecting duct. Which cells lose their aldosterone response?
A researcher measures a new drug: 50 mg/min is filtered, and 120 mg/min appears in the urine. What must the renal tubule be doing with it?
options: Filtering it a second time in the collecting duct

q: Fluid entering the nephron loop is about 300 mOsm/L. Fluid leaving the thick ascending limb is about 100 mOsm/L. What makes it dilute?
options: The descending limb adds water to the tubular fluid
The thick ascending limb removes salt but not water
The thick ascending limb secretes water into the tubule

q: Which route across the tubule wall passes between cells, through the tight junctions?
Name the pinned region.

fig.alt: A strip across the wall of the proximal tubule. On the left is the pale lumen of the tubule, bordered by a wavy brush border; in the middle is one large tubule cell; to the right is a narrow blue band of interstitial space, then a red blood vessel labeled bloodstream. Arrows show H+ leaving the cell into the lumen in exchange for Na+ entering, and Na+ entering the cell together with Cl−, Ca2+, amino acids, glucose and phosphate; these then continue across the cell and interstitial space into the blood. Mg2+ enters the cell, and water crosses all the way to the blood. At the top right, an ATP-driven pump moves Na+ out of the cell into the interstitial space and K+ into the cell.

q: A person drinks 2 L of water quickly, and ADH release falls. Which water reabsorption falls?
options: Obligatory water reabsorption in the proximal convoluted tubule
Water reabsorption in the descending limb
Facultative water reabsorption in the collecting duct
Water reabsorption in the thick ascending limb

q: A person's PTH release rises. Predict the immediate change in each kidney variable, before blood calcium has had time to rise.

variables.name: Calcium reabsorbed in the distal convoluted tubule
Phosphate reabsorbed in the proximal tubule

q: Fluid reabsorbed by the proximal tubule moves readily from the interstitial fluid into the peritubular capillaries. Which pair of pressures in those capillaries favors this?
options: High hydrostatic and low colloid osmotic pressure
Low hydrostatic and low colloid osmotic pressure
Low hydrostatic and high colloid osmotic pressure
High hydrostatic and high colloid osmotic pressure

q: Disease has damaged a woman's renal medulla, so the interstitial fluid at the papilla now reaches only 600 mOsm/L. Her ADH is very high. About what is the most concentrated urine she can make?

variables.name: Aquaporins in the apical membranes of principal cells
Water reabsorbed from the collecting duct

q: A patient with fluid overload is given a loop diuretic. Predict the change in each variable over the next few hours.

variables.name: NaCl reabsorbed by the thick ascending limb

q: A roofer sweats heavily all afternoon without drinking. Sweat has less salt than plasma. Predict the change in each variable across the nervous, endocrine and urinary systems by the end of the afternoon.

variables.name: Aquaporins in collecting duct principal cells

q: Put the steps in order, from a rise in plasma osmolarity to concentrated urine.
options: Hypothalamic osmoreceptors sense the rise in osmolarity
The posterior pituitary releases ADH into the blood
ADH binds its receptor protein on the basolateral membrane of principal cells
cAMP rises and protein kinase A is activated
Vesicles carrying aquaporins fuse with the apical membrane
Water leaves the collecting duct into the salty medulla

q: Imagine the vasa recta were replaced by capillaries that ran straight from the cortex to the papilla and drained there, with the same blood flow. What would happen to the medullary osmotic gradient?

It would stay the same, since the loops, not the vessels, build it

q: What is the osmolarity of the interstitial fluid near the tip of a renal papilla in a person making concentrated urine?

options: NKCC2 pumping salt out of the thick ascending limb
Urea diffusing out of the inner medullary collecting duct
Glucose reabsorption in the proximal tubule
Opposite flow in the two limbs of the nephron loop
Aquaporins in the thick ascending limb
The hairpin shape of the vasa recta

q: A student described the countercurrent multiplier. One step is wrong. Which one?
options: The thick ascending limb pumps NaCl into the interstitial fluid
The descending limb loses water to the saltier interstitial fluid
The descending limb pumps salt in from the interstitial fluid
Flow carries the more concentrated fluid around the bend into the ascending limb
Repeated pumping and flow make the bottom of the loop reach about 1,200 mOsm/L

q: Fill the gap. Fluid in the descending limb becomes more concentrated as it moves deeper into the medulla, because it loses ____ to the salty interstitial fluid.

options: At the tip of the nephron loop
At the end of the proximal tubule
At the start of the distal convoluted tubule
At the end of the collecting duct

fig.alt: A graph of the osmolarity of the fluid inside the tubule, from 0 to 1,300 mOsm/L, at seven points along the nephron from left to right: start of the proximal tubule, end of the proximal tubule, tip of the nephron loop, start of the distal tubule, end of the distal tubule, end of the cortical collecting duct, and end of the collecting duct. A shaded band marks the points that lie in the renal medulla. The fluid is 300 at the start and still 300 at the end of the proximal tubule. It climbs to 1,200 at the tip of the loop, deep in the medulla, then falls to about 100 by the start of the distal tubule and stays about 100 through it. There the line splits. With high ADH, it rises to 300 by the end of the cortical collecting duct and to 1,200 at the end of the collecting duct. With no ADH, shown dashed, it falls to about 50. A dotted line at 300 marks the osmolarity of plasma.

q: On the graph, the fluid is 300 mOsm/L at both the start and the end of the proximal tubule, even though two thirds of the filtrate is reabsorbed there. Why doesn't its osmolarity change?
options: The proximal tubule reabsorbs no solute
Water and solute are reabsorbed in the same proportion
The proximal tubule secretes water to balance the solute it reabsorbs
ADH keeps the proximal tubule's osmolarity fixed

fig.alt: A graph of the osmolarity of the fluid inside the tubule, from 0 to 1,300 mOsm/L, at seven points along the nephron from left to right: start of the proximal tubule, end of the proximal tubule, tip of the nephron loop, start of the distal tubule, end of the distal tubule, end of the cortical collecting duct, and end of the collecting duct. A shaded band marks the points that lie in the renal medulla. The fluid is 300 at the start and still 300 at the end of the proximal tubule. It climbs to 1,200 at the tip of the loop, deep in the medulla, then falls to about 100 by the start of the distal tubule and stays about 100 through it. There the line splits. With high ADH, it rises to 300 by the end of the cortical collecting duct and to 1,200 at the end of the collecting duct. With no ADH, shown dashed, it falls to about 50. A dotted line at 300 marks the osmolarity of plasma.

q: Leo, 6, passes about 5 L of pale urine a day and is always thirsty. His blood glucose is normal. His ADH level is high, and an injection of synthetic ADH does not reduce his urine volume. Where is the fault most likely to be?
options: His posterior pituitary releases too little ADH
His collecting duct cells can't respond to ADH
His glomeruli filter too much fluid
His thick ascending limbs pump too much salt

q: Mrs. Park, 64, has high blood pressure, and calcium stones have formed in her kidneys twice. Her doctor chooses a diuretic that lowers blood pressure and also reduces the calcium in her urine. Which kind?
options: A drug that blocks ADH's receptor protein

q: Mr. Adeyemi, 71, has heart failure and takes furosemide, a loop diuretic. His plasma potassium has fallen to 3.1 mmol/L. How does the drug cause this?
options: It blocks potassium reabsorption in the proximal tubule
It lowers aldosterone, which normally keeps potassium
It pumps potassium directly into the urine
It sends more sodium and fluid to the principal cells

q: People who eat very little protein for months can't concentrate their urine as fully as others. Why?
options: Their inner medulla has less urea
They make less ADH, since ADH is a protein
Their thick ascending limbs lose their NKCC2 carriers

q: Name the pinned structure.

fig.alt: A strip across the wall of a collecting duct. On the left, the pale yellow lumen labeled lumen of collecting tubule, with water shown as blue arrows. In the middle, two stacked cells labeled collecting tubule cell; round storage vesicles studded with pink dots, the aquaporins, sit inside them. In the upper cell only two aquaporins sit in the membrane facing the lumen and two water arrows enter. In the lower cell, dotted arrows show vesicles fusing with that membrane, labeled aquaporin pores are inserted into cell membrane, increasing flow of water out of the tubule, and four water arrows enter. Water leaves both cells through aquaporins on the far side, crosses a thin blue band labeled interstitial fluid, and enters a red vessel labeled bloodstream and plasma.

q: A patient with a swollen brain after a head injury is given mannitol, which is filtered but not reabsorbed. Why does her urine output rise?
options: Mannitol blocks NKCC2 in the thick ascending limb of the loop
Mannitol stays in the tubule and holds water there by osmosis
Mannitol lowers ADH release from the posterior pituitary
Mannitol blocks aldosterone's receptor protein on principal cells

q: Which statement correctly compares the countercurrent multiplier and the countercurrent exchanger?
options: The multiplier uses energy to build the gradient; the exchanger passively preserves it
The exchanger uses energy to build the gradient; the multiplier is passive and preserves it
Both use energy directly: one in the nephron loop and the other in the collecting duct
Both are passive; the gradient comes from ADH

q: A patient's urine creatinine is 90 mg/dL, her urine flow is 1.5 mL/min and her plasma creatinine is 1.0 mg/dL. What is her creatinine clearance?
A man collects 2,880 mL of urine in 24 hours. His urine creatinine is 60 mg/dL and his plasma creatinine is 1.5 mg/dL. What is his creatinine clearance?
In a healthy person, the renal clearance of a nutrient is 0 mL/min even though it is freely filtered. What does that mean?
options: It is secreted and reabsorbed equally
It is filtered, then all of it is reabsorbed
It is broken down by enzymes in the bladder urine

q: A person's GFR is 120 mL/min. A drug that is freely filtered has a renal clearance of 40 mL/min. What does the tubule do with it overall?
options: It can't be judged without the urine volume

q: Mr. Haas, 66, had a plasma creatinine of 1.0 mg/dL a year ago. It is now steady at 2.0 mg/dL. His muscle mass hasn't changed. About how has his GFR changed?
options: It has fallen by only about 10%
It has fallen by about half

q: Why does creatinine clearance run about 10 to 20% higher than the true GFR?
options: The proximal tubule secretes a little creatinine
Creatinine is made inside the kidney tubule
Plasma proteins carry creatinine into the filtrate

q: A man loses 1.5 L of blood in a car crash. Predict the change in each variable across the cardiovascular, nervous, endocrine and urinary systems over the first hour.
Select every hormone the kidney itself makes.
Which hormone makes the kidney excrete more potassium while keeping more sodium?
A tumor makes a person's parathyroid glands release too much PTH. How does their urine change?
options: More phosphate and less calcium, at first
More water and lower specific gravity

q: Ms. Bell, 27, has had burning on urination and a frequent urge to void for two days. She has no fever or flank pain. Her dipstick is positive for nitrite and leukocyte esterase. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: A kidney stone blocking one of the ureters
Urinary tract infection of the bladder

q: After a hot marathon, a runner passes a small amount of dark yellow urine with a specific gravity of 1.030. What does this show?
options: Her kidneys are making concentrated urine, with high ADH

q: An adult patient's urine output over 24 hours is 250 mL. What is this called?
Put the steps of pressure natriuresis in order.
options: Pressure in the peritubular capillaries and kidney interstitial fluid rises
The proximal tubule reabsorbs less sodium
More sodium and water leave in the urine
Blood volume falls, and arterial pressure comes back down

q: Mrs. Tran, 70, has stage 4 chronic kidney disease. She is pale and tired, and her hemoglobin is 9 g/dL. Her iron and vitamin B12 levels are normal. What most likely explains her anemia?
options: Her kidneys filter red blood cells into the urine
Her kidneys make too little erythropoietin
Her kidneys make too much renin

q: Mr. Diallo, 59, on hemodialysis, misses two sessions and comes in weak, with a plasma potassium of 7.2 mmol/L. Which consequence is the most immediate danger?
A student described hemodialysis. One step is wrong. Which one?
options: Blood is pumped through a filter beside a semipermeable membrane
Dialysate flows on the other side of the membrane
Urea diffuses from the dialysate into the blood
Potassium diffuses from the blood into the dialysate
Excess water is removed by pressure across the membrane

q: A man has passed two calcium oxalate stones. What single change most lowers his risk of another?
options: Passing more than about 2.5 L of urine a day
Cutting all calcium from his diet
Drinking less so his urine is more concentrated

q: Mrs. Okafor, 45, has had three children. She leaks small spurts of urine when she coughs or lifts her toddler, but never feels a sudden urge. Which type of incontinence is this, and what is the first treatment?
options: Urge incontinence; drugs that relax the detrusor
Overflow incontinence; a catheter to drain the bladder
Stress incontinence; pelvic floor muscle training
Functional incontinence; help reaching the toilet

q: After three days of vomiting, Mr. Lind, 80, takes high doses of ibuprofen for a painful knee. His urine output falls and his creatinine rises. How did the ibuprofen contribute?
options: It blocked prostaglandins that were protecting his GFR
It blocked NKCC2 and caused a large water loss
It raised his ADH, stopping urine flow
It crystallized in his ureters and blocked them

q: Complete the renal clearance formula: C = (U × V) ÷ ____.

A woman who bled heavily after an injury has a low urine output and a rising creatinine. Her kidney tissue is healthy, and her output recovers once blood is transfused. How is her acute kidney injury classified?
Name the pinned molecule.

fig.alt: Ball-and-stick models of three molecules, with nitrogen atoms in blue, carbon in black, oxygen in red and hydrogen in white. Left, labeled ammonia: one nitrogen bonded to three hydrogens. Middle, labeled urea: a central carbon double-bonded to an oxygen and bonded to two nitrogens, each carrying two hydrogens. Right, labeled uric acid, much larger: two fused rings of carbon and nitrogen atoms, a six-membered ring and a five-membered ring, with three oxygens and four hydrogens attached around the edge.
